summary:
RotaDF: satellite-based crop rotation advice for farmers in Brazil’s Federal District

We built RotaDF, a web app that helps small and medium farmers in the Federal District (Brasília) decide what to plant in the dry season after soybeans. The farmer draws their land on a satellite map, says how they farm today, what matters most to them (saving water, protecting soil, income or fertility) and their soil type. The app first checks whether the area can be farmed at all. It flags buildings, water, wetlands, native vegetation and protected parks using Dynamic World, JRC Global Surface Water and WDPA. It then reads the land’s condition from NASA data: MODIS vegetation, GPM rainfall, SRTM terrain, HLS imagery, plus Sentinel-1 radar that sees through clouds. On top of that it detects El Niño or La Niña from NOAA’s ONI index and checks Brazil’s official planting-risk calendar (ZARC) for Brasília. Together, these produce a simple, ranked recommendation in plain Portuguese.

This matters because farmers usually make this choice without seeing climate, risk and land data together. Planting outside ZARC dates can void crop insurance, and El Niño years bring irregular rain. RotaDF turns open NASA and government data into a decision a farmer can act on.
details:
Project details

What it does and how it works

RotaDF is a web app for farmers in Brazil's Federal District. It answers one question: what should I plant after soybeans in the dry season? The app compares four rotation options:

  • Soybeans followed by fallow (resting land)
  • Soybeans followed by second-crop corn (safrinha)
  • Soybeans followed by corn intercropped with brachiaria grass
  • Soybeans followed by cover crops (millet or crotalaria)

The farmer draws their field on a satellite map and answers three short questions: what they plant now, what matters most to them, and their soil type. The app then works through four steps:

  1. Can this land be farmed? It uses Dynamic World land cover (Sentinel-2, 10 m), JRC Global Surface Water and the WDPA protected-areas database. Buildings, water, wetlands, native vegetation and strictly protected parks lead to a green (suitable), yellow (with restrictions) or red (not recommended) verdict. Yellow verdicts also include an estimate of the plantable hectares.
    • NASA MODIS NDVI for vegetation health
    • NASA GPM IMERG for rainfall
    • NASA SRTM for slope
    • NASA HLS imagery for the map layer
    • Sentinel-1 radar with a Lee speckle filter, which sees through clouds
  2. What is the climate this year? It detects El Niño or La Niña live from NOAA's Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), using NOAA's official thresholds and persistence rule.
  3. When is it safe to plant? It uses Brazil's official agricultural risk zoning (ZARC, from the Ministry of Agriculture) for Brasília. It checks whether a soybean crop followed by a second crop fits the calendar for the farmer's soil type.

All of this feeds a scoring model weighted by the farmer's priority. The result is a ranked recommendation in plain Portuguese, with the reasons, the precautions and a planting calendar.

Benefits

  • It brings climate, official risk and land data that farmers normally see separately into one place.
  • It helps farmers stay inside ZARC planting windows, which are required for crop insurance and Proagro, Brazil's federal crop-loss program.
  • It adjusts automatically in El Niño years. For example, it only accepts 20%-risk planting dates and gives more weight to saving water and keeping soil covered.
  • It warns before anyone plants on water, wetlands, urban land or protected areas.

Intended impact

  • Fewer crop losses from badly timed second crops.
  • Less soil erosion.
  • Better use of water.
  • Data-driven decisions for farmers who don't have agronomists or GIS tools, while still pointing them to Emater-DF (the Federal District's rural extension agency) for validation.

Tools and technologies

  • Language: Python.
  • App and maps: Streamlit, Folium and streamlit-folium.
    • NASA: MODIS, GPM IMERG, SRTM, HLS
    • ESA Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 (through Dynamic World)
    • JRC Global Surface Water
    • WDPA protected areas
    • NOAA CPC ONI index
    • MAPA ZARC open data (Brazil's Ministry of Agriculture)
  • Development: a standard Windows laptop, with AI coding assistance (Claude Code). No special hardware was needed.

Creativity

  • It combines three kinds of signals that rarely appear together in a farmer-facing tool: global ocean temperatures (El Niño and La Niña), a national legal risk calendar (ZARC) and field-level satellite data.
  • It checks whether a soybean crop and a second crop fit the official calendar back to back, not just whether each crop fits on its own.
  • It answers "can I farm here at all?" before giving any advice.
  • The interface uses plain language, traffic-light indicators and simple soil descriptions, so a farmer does not need to know the technical terms.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility: simple Portuguese, few inputs, and a map the farmer can draw on.
    • The scoring weights and thresholds are heuristics that still need validation with Emater-DF and Embrapa (Brazil's agricultural research agency).
    • Harvest dates are estimated from the soybean maturity group.
    • The app does not consider soil chemistry, prices or costs.
  • Reliability: if NOAA cannot be reached, the app still runs and marks the El Niño data as unavailable. The ZARC data is stored in the project, so it works offline.
